Q001587:
Why this is correct:
A cache policy for /api/* whose cache key includes only the session-relevant value keeps responses correctly separated while maximizing cache hits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Forward all query strings in the cache key: fragments the cache.
• Origin request policy only: doesn't change the cache key.
• Disable caching: loses all offload.

Key takeaway: keep cache keys minimal but correct.
Q001588:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes custom UDP traffic over the AWS backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB: HTTP only.
• Route 53 latency: DNS only, no acceleration.
• CloudFront: HTTP(S).

Key takeaway: global UDP → Global Accelerator.
Q001590:
Why this is correct:
Origin groups fail over only on the status codes listed in the failover criteria. If 403 isn't included, CloudFront won't fail over on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TCP-only failover: status codes are supported.
• No S3 origins: S3 is supported.
• OAC blocked on secondary: would fail after failover, not prevent it.

Key takeaway: include the right status codes in failover criteria.
Q001591:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront Functions can't make network calls. Lambda@Edge on origin-request can call the external API and act on its response.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Functions with outbound calls: not supported.
• Functions on origin-response: Functions run only on viewer events.
• Origin-request unsupported: it's supported for Lambda@Edge.

Key takeaway: network calls at the edge → Lambda@Edge.
Q001592:
Why this is correct:
A custom routing accelerator maps listener port ranges to specific EC2 destinations, letting clients reach individual game servers behind a few static IPs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SOURCE_IP affinity: doesn't target specific servers.
• EIP endpoints: standard accelerators balance, not map.
• NLB endpoint: balances across targets.

Key takeaway: deterministic mapping to specific instances → custom routing accelerator.
Q001593:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront evaluates cache behaviors in the listed precedence order. Move /images/* above broader patterns so it matches first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic specificity ordering: not applied.
• Trailing wildcard invalid: it's valid.
• Separate precedence field in another setting: order is the precedence.

Key takeaway: behavior order = precedence.
Q001595:
Why this is correct:
Origin Shield adds a central caching layer near the origin, collapsing requests from edge locations and reducing load on the on-premises origin.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Second distribution: doubles origin load.
• Signed URLs: access control.
• Field-level encryption: data protection.

Key takeaway: protect a constrained origin → Origin Shield.
Q001597:
Why this is correct:
Geoproximity routing with a bias expands or shrinks the area routed to each Region, shifting traffic gradually (configured via Traffic Flow).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency without health checks: no control over shift.
• Fewer geolocation records: coarse.
• Simple routing: no control.

Key takeaway: shift geographic boundaries → geoproximity bias.
Q001598:
Why this is correct:
A Resolver inbound endpoint receives queries forwarded from on-premises DNS (via conditional forwarders) and resolves the private hosted zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: exposes records.
• DNS64 on VPN: unrelated.
• Outbound endpoint: for VPC to on-premises.

Key takeaway: on-prem → AWS private zones = inbound endpoint.
Q001599:
Why this is correct:
Completing the DNSSEC chain of trust requires adding Route 53's DS record at the parent zone through the registrar.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Nothing more: the parent must have the DS record.
• Rotate the ZSK: unrelated.
• CNAME to a KMS ARN: meaningless.

Key takeaway: DNSSEC needs the DS record in the parent.
Q001600:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocks queries to domains in block lists for VPCs while allowing others.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs with Lambda: reactive.
• SG FQDN rules: not supported.
• Network Firewall only: works for traffic, but DNS Firewall directly blocks resolution.

Key takeaway: block malicious domain resolution → DNS Firewall.
Q001601:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 health checkers must reach the endpoint. If the security group blocks their IP ranges, the check fails or behaves unexpectedly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low secondary TTL: speeds failover.
• Private zones don't support failover: they do (with CloudWatch-alarm checks).
• No health checks on primary: required.

Key takeaway: allow Route 53 health checker IPs.
Q001602:
Why this is correct:
A shared Resolver rule must also be associated with each VPC that should use it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IP per VPC: not required.
• RAM doesn't share rules: it does.
• Endpoint SGs: would affect all VPCs.

Key takeaway: share and then associate Resolver rules.
Q001604:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account PHZ association: Account A creates a VPC association authorization for B's VPC, and Account B associates the VPC with the zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recreate zone as shared: not needed.
• Share VPC with RAM: not needed.
• Add CIDR: not how PHZ works.

Key takeaway: cross-account PHZ = authorize (owner) + associate (VPC owner).
Q001605:
Why this is correct:
Latency routing chooses among existing records. Without an ap-southeast-1 record, Australian users get the lowest-latency existing Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• First record preferred: false.
• Three records needed: false.
• DNS Firewall caching: unrelated.

Key takeaway: add a latency record for each endpoint Region.
Q001606:
Why this is correct:
An NLB preserves the client source IP at Layer 4 for most target types, so the application sees it without parsing headers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB re-encrypting with ACM: not the reason.
• ALB X-Forwarded-For: requires header parsing.
• ALB proxy protocol v2: ALB doesn't send it.

Key takeaway: client IP at L4 → NLB.
Q001607:
Why this is correct:
Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts and scales third-party appliances in the traffic path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB with Lambda: not appliances.
• CLB with ASG: not transparent.
• NLB UDP: not transparent insertion.

Key takeaway: inline appliances → GWLB.
Q001608:
Why this is correct:
Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all targets, but NLB cross-AZ traffic incurs data transfer charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't change: configurable.
• Disables client IP preservation: no.
• Free and only health checks: incorrect.

Key takeaway: NLB cross-zone = even load vs. cross-AZ cost.
Q001609:
Why this is correct:
If /health doesn't exist, all targets fail health checks. Restore /status or implement a working /health endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Healthy threshold: doesn't fix a 404.
• Deregistration delay: unrelated.
• 300-second timeout: invalid and irrelevant.

Key takeaway: health check path must exist.
Q001611:
Why this is correct:
A longer deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish before targets are removed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cross-zone: unrelated.
• Shorter interval: unrelated.
• Switch to NLB: same issue.

Key takeaway: graceful removal → deregistration delay.
Q001614:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the TGW attachment keeps both directions of a flow on the same AZ, so the same stateful appliance sees the whole flow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source-IP stickiness: GWLB already hashes flows; asymmetry comes from TGW.
• Cross-zone on GWLB: doesn't fix TGW asymmetry.
• NAT per AZ: unrelated.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection via TGW → appliance mode.
Q001615:
Why this is correct:
NLB TLS passthrough keeps encryption end to end but gives up Layer 7 features. ALB termination enables L7 routing and WAF, with re-encryption to targets optional.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB can't handle TLS: it can.
• ALB always end-to-end: it terminates.
• No difference: they differ.

Key takeaway: passthrough vs. L7 features.
Q001617:
Why this is correct:
Resolver query logging records DNS queries from VPCs and can send them to a central destination (S3, CloudWatch Logs, Firehose), shared across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: not DNS queries.
• Flow log DNS fields: not available.
• DNS Firewall alerts only: only matched queries.

Key takeaway: all DNS queries → Resolver query logging.
Q001618:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager's global network registers TGWs, sites, and connections, giving a global topology view with monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reachability Analyzer per TGW: not global.
• Manual dashboards: toil.
• Config aggregator: configuration.

Key takeaway: global network visibility → Network Manager.
Q001619:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Network Monitor probes measure packet loss and latency continuously between AWS and on-premises destinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX metrics only: link-level.
• Flow Logs with Athena: no latency or loss.
• Route Analyzer: route analysis.

Key takeaway: hybrid path latency/loss → Network Monitor.
Q001621:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway Flow Logs capture traffic the TGW itself processes, including drops, to diagnose attachment-to-attachment issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• VPC Flow Logs capture TGW natively: not TGW decisions.
• Resolver logs: DNS.

Key takeaway: TGW traffic visibility → TGW Flow Logs.
Q001622:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager Route Analyzer analyzes TGW routes to show whether a path exists or where a route is missing or blackholed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no.
• Logs Insights on flow logs: traffic, not routes.
• Reachability Analyzer only: VPC-focused paths; Route Analyzer targets TGW routes.

Key takeaway: TGW route problems → Route Analyzer.
Q001623:
Why this is correct:
TGW publishes per-attachment metrics such as BytesIn, BytesOut, and PacketDropCount, which CloudWatch alarms can monitor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 request metrics: unrelated.
• EC2 CPU: unrelated.
• Route 53 health checks: unrelated.

Key takeaway: attachment health → TGW CloudWatch metrics.
Q001624:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs can be delivered directly to a central S3 bucket whose policy allows delivery from all organization accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't deliver cross-account: they can.
• Manual weekly copies: toil.
• Email: no.

Key takeaway: central flow logs → org-wide bucket policy.
Q001626:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway with a transit VIF, associated with each Region's Transit Gateway, extends one connection to VPCs in multiple Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Five private VIFs sharing a BGP session: not how VIFs work.
• Hosted VIF per Region: unnecessary.
• SiteLink: site-to-site over the backbone.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway.
Q001627:
Why this is correct:
AS path prepending on routes advertised over Connection B makes that path less preferred for traffic from AWS, so Connection A carries it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keepalive interval: failure detection.
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.
• Static route on AWS side: not configurable this way.

Key takeaway: influence AWS→on-prem path → AS path prepend.
Q001628:
Why this is correct:
Running BGP on both paths and prepending the AS path on VPN advertisements makes DX preferred with automatic failover to VPN.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual VPN enabling: slow.
• Static VPN routes: may be preferred unexpectedly.
• Same ASN: not a preference mechanism.

Key takeaway: DX primary + VPN backup = BGP with prepending on VPN.
Q001629:
Why this is correct:
Direct Connect SiteLink connects on-premises sites through DX locations over the AWS global network without going through a Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway with private VIFs: connects to VPCs, not site-to-site.
• Global Accelerator custom routing: not site-to-site.
• TGW peering: VPC traffic.

Key takeaway: site-to-site via DX locations → SiteLink.
Q001630:
Why this is correct:
MACsec provides Layer 2 encryption on supported dedicated connections (such as 10 and 100 Gbps).

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS at the router: not L2.
• IPsec on hosted connections: L3, not L2.
• MACsec only on hosted connections: it's for dedicated connections.

Key takeaway: L2 encryption on DX → MACsec.
Q001631:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway Connect attachments use GRE with BGP for high-throughput integration with SD-WAN appliances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transit VIF: DX, not SD-WAN overlay.
• Standard VPN: lower throughput.
• Peering: not a TGW attachment for SD-WAN.

Key takeaway: SD-WAN to TGW → Connect attachments.
Q001632:
Why this is correct:
BFD detects link failures in under a second, working alongside BGP for fast failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routing: loses dynamic failover.
• ECMP: load sharing.
• Longer hold timer: slower detection.

Key takeaway: fast failure detection → BFD.
Q001634:
Why this is correct:
VPN tunnels don't support jumbo frames. When traffic fails over from DX to VPN, 9001-byte packets fail unless MTU is lowered or path MTU discovery works.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual re-establishment: not required.
• BGP can't fail over: it can.
• TGW VPN no BGP: it supports BGP.

Key takeaway: plan MTU for the backup path.
Q001635:
Why this is correct:
A Transit Gateway gives hub-and-spoke any-to-any connectivity that scales as VPCs grow.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway per VPC: for on-premises.
• Full mesh peering: grows as n².
• One shared VPC: loses account separation.

Key takeaway: many VPCs any-to-any → TGW.
Q001637:
Why this is correct:
Spokes route 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW, which routes it to the central egress VPC with NAT gateways (and return routes back).

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT in every spoke: not centralized.
• VPC endpoints for internet: not possible.
• Peering for 0.0.0.0/0: peering isn't transitive for internet egress.

Key takeaway: central egress → TGW default route to egress VPC.
Q001639:
Why this is correct:
Each VPC's subnet route table must send the other VPC's CIDR to the TGW. Missing subnet routes are a common cause.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static routes required: propagation works.
• Multicast: unrelated.
• Same AZ: not required.

Key takeaway: TGW needs routes in VPC and TGW route tables.
Q001640:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment keeps flows symmetric through the same AZ and appliance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multicast: unrelated.
• Second TGW: unnecessary.
• Cross-zone on TGW: not a setting.

Key takeaway: stateful inspection + TGW → appliance mode.
Q001641:
Why this is correct:
TGW peering attachments don't support route propagation. Add static routes pointing to the peering attachment in each TGW's route table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering instead: loses hub model.
• PrivateLink between TGWs: no.
• Automatic propagation: not supported.

Key takeaway: TGW peering = static routes.
Q001642:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway multicast domains deliver one stream to multiple receivers (IGMPv2 or static membership).

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW Connect: SD-WAN.
• Broadcast mode peering: doesn't exist.
• Flow log filter: logging.

Key takeaway: multicast on AWS → TGW multicast.
Q001645:
Why this is correct:
Each LAG member connection needs its own MACsec CKN/CAK association.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared session at LAG level: no.
• One member only: all members need keys.
• Hosted connections: MACsec is for dedicated.

Key takeaway: MACsec keys per member.
Q001646:
Why this is correct:
With must-secure mode, traffic flows only if MACsec is established. A CKN/CAK mismatch between the router and AWS blocks traffic on that member.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't enable per member: you can.
• Minimum links: would affect the whole LAG.
• BGP local preference: not member-level.

Key takeaway: must-secure + key mismatch = no traffic.
Q001647:
Why this is correct:
Prepending the AS path on routes advertised from on-premises over Connection B makes AWS prefer Connection A for return traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower MED on A: MED isn't compared across different locations reliably.
• Local preference on B: affects on-prem outbound.
• Prepend from AWS: you don't control AWS advertisements.

Key takeaway: steer AWS→on-prem traffic by prepending your advertisements.
Q001648:
Why this is correct:
AWS supports BGP local preference communities. Tagging VIF B routes with the low local-preference community makes AWS prefer VIF A.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.
• Support case: not needed.
• Static route with admin distance: not available.

Key takeaway: control AWS path selection with communities.
Q001649:
Why this is correct:
MED is compared only between routes from the same neighboring AS. If the paths come from different ASNs, MED doesn't influence selection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• iBGP preference: not the case.
• Higher MED preferred: lower is preferred.
• No MED support: MED is supported.

Key takeaway: MED works within one neighbor AS.
Q001650:
Why this is correct:
On the customer router, higher local preference wins before AS path length, so that path is chosen.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both installed: not by default.
• AS path first: local preference comes before.
• MED first: MED comes later.

Key takeaway: BGP order: local preference → AS path → MED.
Q001652:
Why this is correct:
If traffic doesn't fail over, the customer gateway may keep advertising routes over the dead tunnel. The device must withdraw them (for example, by detecting the tunnel down).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two active tunnels unsupported: supported.
• Same device required: no.
• Propagated routes need manual action: no.

Key takeaway: failover requires route withdrawal.
Q001653:
Why this is correct:
BGP propagates prefix changes automatically, without manual route updates on either side.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BGP needed for AES-256: no.
• Static lower latency: no.
• BGP only option for ECMP: not the key difference asked.

Key takeaway: dynamic routing reduces manual changes.
Q001654:
Why this is correct:
The High Resiliency model uses one connection at each of two DX locations, surviving a location failure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dev/test: single location.
• LAG at one location: single location.
• Maximum Resiliency: works, but costs more than needed for the requirement.

Key takeaway: tolerate location failure → two locations.
Q001655:
Why this is correct:
Maximum Resiliency requires separate connections on separate devices at separate locations, not two ports on one device.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Combine into LAG: still one device.
• BGP issue: not the design gap.
• Only two router interfaces: ignores AWS side.

Key takeaway: resiliency depends on device and location diversity.
Q001656:
Why this is correct:
High Resiliency survives a location loss. Maximum Resiliency adds device redundancy within each location, surviving device failures too.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped protections: incorrect.
• Location counts wrong: incorrect.
• Same thing: different.

Key takeaway: Maximum = High + device redundancy.
Q001657:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode keeps return traffic on the same AZ and inspection appliance for centralized egress through a TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW Connect: SD-WAN.
• Jumbo frames: MTU.
• Multicast: unrelated.

Key takeaway: symmetric inspection → appliance mode.
Q001658:
Why this is correct:
A new attachment needs a TGW route table association and propagation (or static routes) so other VPCs learn its CIDR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 24-hour refresh: false.
• SG blocks propagation: SGs don't affect routes.
• DX required: false.

Key takeaway: TGW routes need association and propagation.
Q001659:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway multicast delivers to receivers in VPCs attached to the same TGW whose subnets are associated with the multicast domain.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ELB multicast: not supported.
• Route 53 multicast: doesn't exist.
• Peering multicast: not supported.

Key takeaway: multicast scope = same TGW, associated subnets.
Q001660:
Why this is correct:
Inter-Region TGW peering connects Regions, and a DX gateway associated with each Region's TGW gives on-premises access (TGW peering doesn't propagate DX routes).

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering because TGW can't: TGW peering supports inter-Region.
• DX gateway only same Region: it associates across Regions.
• Automatic DX route propagation over peering: no.

Key takeaway: combine TGW peering with DX gateway associations.
Q001662:
Why this is correct:
Clients use the public name only if private DNS is enabled on the endpoint and the service has a verified private DNS name.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG blocks DNS: DNS isn't through the endpoint SG.
• Endpoints never override DNS: private DNS does.
• Recreate as gateway endpoint: not possible.

Key takeaway: private DNS makes endpoints transparent.
Q001663:
Why this is correct:
A Gateway Load Balancer endpoint (a PrivateLink endpoint type) inserts the appliance transparently in the traffic path through route tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GWLB can't use PrivateLink: it does via GWLB endpoints.
• Gateway VPC endpoint: only S3/DynamoDB.
• Standard interface endpoint: not inline routing.

Key takeaway: transparent inline inspection → GWLB endpoint.
Q001664:
Why this is correct:
VPC sharing through AWS RAM lets application accounts launch resources into centrally managed subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: separate VPCs.
• Roles into the networking account: resources land in the wrong account.
• Copying CIDRs: creates separate, possibly overlapping VPCs.

Key takeaway: central subnets for many accounts → RAM sharing.
Q001665:
Why this is correct:
Participants still need IAM permissions (such as ec2:RunInstances) in their own account to launch into shared subnets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Read-only shares: subnet shares aren't read-only.
• DNS attribute needed for sharing: no.
• Same Region: shares are Regional, but that's not the likely cause.

Key takeaway: shared subnets still need participant IAM.
Q001666:
Why this is correct:
Within an organization, RAM sharing can be automatic (no invitations). Accounts outside it must be specified individually and accept invitations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Merge orgs: not required.
• Cross-org impossible: possible with invitations.
• TGWs can't be shared: they can.

Key takeaway: RAM: org sharing is seamless; external needs invitations.
Q001667:
Why this is correct:
An IPAM hierarchy with a top-level pool and Regional child pools delegated to teams allocates non-overlapping CIDRs everywhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single global pool only: hierarchies are supported.
• Flat pools per team: overlaps possible.
• Separate IPAMs per Region: no global view.

Key takeaway: org-wide addressing → IPAM pool hierarchy.
Q001668:
Why this is correct:
IPAM prevents overlap only for CIDRs allocated from its pools. A manually specified CIDR can overlap; IPAM will flag it for monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allows /24 overlaps: no.
• Only across orgs: no.
• No overlap checks: it checks pool allocations.

Key takeaway: enforce allocation from IPAM pools.
Q001669:
Why this is correct:
After BYOIP onboarding, provision the range into a public-scope IPAM pool to manage allocations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic import: not automatic.
• IPAM only private: it has a public scope.
• Convert to private: no.

Key takeaway: BYOIP management → public-scope IPAM pools.
Q001671:
Why this is correct:
Resolver uses the most specific matching rule associated with the VPC. If the more specific rule isn't associated with that VPC, the broader rule applies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alphabetical: no.
• Single-label only: no.
• No parent/child overlap: allowed.

Key takeaway: most specific associated rule wins.
Q001672:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall evaluates queries from the VPC before forwarding, so a blocked domain is blocked even if a forwarding rule exists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only internet-bound: it filters all Resolver queries.
• SERVFAIL always: depends on the block response configured.
• Forwarding always wins: no.

Key takeaway: DNS Firewall applies before forwarding.
Q001673:
Why this is correct:
An inbound Resolver endpoint accepts queries from on-premises DNS servers configured to forward the zone to it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound endpoint: VPC to on-premises.
• Directory Service: not required.
• Public zone duplicate: exposes names.

Key takeaway: on-prem resolving private zones → inbound endpoint.
Q001674:
Why this is correct:
After a rule is shared, the spoke account's principal needs route53resolver:AssociateResolverRule permission to associate it with a VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cross-Region limitation: not the cause.
• Only inbound rules: forwarding rules share fine.
• CLI only: console works too.

Key takeaway: sharing isn't enough; associating needs IAM.
Q001675:
Why this is correct:
Central inbound and outbound endpoints and forwarding rules in a DNS account, shared through RAM and associated with all VPCs, provide hybrid DNS without per-VPC endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zones: expose names.
• Endpoints per VPC: costly.
• Can't centralize: they can.

Key takeaway: centralize hybrid DNS in one account.
Q001676:
Why this is correct:
A private hosted zone with the same name as the public zone gives VPC clients internal answers (split-horizon). Records needed in both must exist in both zones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split-horizon impossible: it's supported.
• Geolocation for VPC vs. public: not how it works.
• VPC-only mode on public zone: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: split-horizon → same-name private + public zones.
Q001678:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall blocks resolution of disallowed domains. Network Firewall inspects actual flows (SNI, HTTP host), catching direct-IP connections too. They complement each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Network Firewall can't filter domains: it can.
• DNS Firewall inspects SNI: it doesn't.
• Identical: different layers.

Key takeaway: DNS layer vs. traffic layer.
Q001680:
Why this is correct:
A manual route matching the new route causes a conflict. Detect drift, then import or remove the manual route so CloudFormation can manage it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route tables immutable: no.
• Too many subnets: unrelated.
• CFN overwrites: it fails instead.

Key takeaway: manual changes cause stack conflicts.
Q001681:
Why this is correct:
A custom CDK construct with a typed props interface packages the attachment logic for reuse with validation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raw JSON nested stack: less reusable.
• Conformance packs: compliance.
• YAML in Parameter Store: hacky.

Key takeaway: reusable infrastructure components → CDK constructs.
Q001682:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed StackSets targeting OUs automatically deploy the baseline to new accounts added to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config aggregators deploy: no.
• Can't target OUs: service-managed can.
• Manual in 150 accounts: toil.

Key takeaway: OU-wide baseline → service-managed StackSets.
Q001684:
Why this is correct:
Register SD-WAN sites, links, and devices in the global network so Network Manager shows them alongside Connect attachments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate SD-WAN service: no.
• Connect attachments invisible: no.
• No site concept: it has sites.

Key takeaway: model on-prem topology in the global network.
Q001685:
Why this is correct:
Network Manager relies on event data and metrics that can lag live state. Confirm current status in the Direct Connect console or router.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Console malfunctioning: unlikely.
• Same value means disconnect: no.
• Can't display DX: it can.

Key takeaway: monitoring views may lag.
Q001686:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress (via CloudTrail) triggers a Lambda that revokes the offending rule within seconds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty modifies SGs: no.
• Inspector revokes rules: no.
• Daily Config report: slow and no remediation.

Key takeaway: real-time SG remediation → EventBridge + Lambda.
Q001687:
Why this is correct:
AccessDenied means the execution role lacks the needed write actions, such as ec2:ReplaceNetworkAclEntry.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move into VPC: unrelated to IAM.
• More memory: unrelated.
• VPC access grants EC2 writes: no.

Key takeaway: AccessDenied → add the specific permissions.
Q001688:
Why this is correct:
Firewall Manager centrally enforces and remediates SG and NACL policies with little code. A custom Config and Lambda pipeline offers more flexibility at more effort.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: they differ.
• Can't combine Config and Lambda: they can.
• Firewall Manager can't remediate: it can.

Key takeaway: managed policy enforcement vs. custom flexibility.
Q001690:
Why this is correct:
The automation should assume a scoped cross-account role that has only the needed Direct Connect permissions in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: over-privileged.
• Can't work cross-account: it can.
• Config aggregators write: they don't.

Key takeaway: least-privilege cross-account automation.
Q001691:
Why this is correct:
Automation runbooks include approval steps and readable, auditable step logs, while Lambda offers general-purpose code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always faster: no.
• Lambda can't call APIs: false.
• Strict superset: no.

Key takeaway: operational runbooks → Automation.
Q001692:
Why this is correct:
Shutting down the primary BGP session on the customer router simulates a failure safely, letting you watch traffic fail over and restore it afterward.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Support disabling ports: not how testing works.
• Deleting the VIF: disruptive.
• MTU change: unrelated.

Key takeaway: test DX failover by disabling BGP on your side.
Q001693:
Why this is correct:
Private VIFs accept a limited number of advertised prefixes (100). Exceeding it takes the BGP session down. Summarize routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DX gateway deleted: different symptom.
• ASN change: different issue.
• BFD incompatible: it's supported.

Key takeaway: too many prefixes → BGP session down.
Q001694:
Why this is correct:
Three route tables: Prod and Dev each learn only Shared routes, and Shared learns both, so Prod and Dev can't reach each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One table: everyone reaches everyone.
• Blackholes in one table: fragile.
• Two tables: doesn't separate cleanly.

Key takeaway: segment with separate TGW route tables.
Q001696:
Why this is correct:
BFD detects link failures in under a second, so ECMP removes a failed path quickly instead of waiting for BGP timers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VGW instead of DX gateway: unrelated.
• Disable propagation: breaks routing.
• Longer hold timer: slower detection.

Key takeaway: fast failover → BFD.
Q001697:
Why this is correct:
Prepending the customer ASN on routes sent over the backup connection makes AWS prefer the primary for return traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher MED on primary: makes it less preferred.
• Lower local preference on primary: affects your outbound.
• More specific on backup: makes backup preferred.

Key takeaway: make backup less attractive with prepending.
Q001698:
Why this is correct:
A TGW route table can't route overlapping CIDRs from two attachments. Re-IP one VPC or use NAT or PrivateLink.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW load-balances overlaps: no.
• MTU mismatch: unrelated.
• Expected disambiguation: no.

Key takeaway: overlapping CIDRs need translation or re-IP.
Q001699:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN tunnel logs capture IKE and IPsec negotiation events that explain periodic drops.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail data events: not tunnel events.
• Traffic Mirroring on CGW: not available.
• Flow logs on VGW: not tunnel negotiation.

Key takeaway: diagnose VPN tunnel drops → tunnel logs.
Q001700:
Why this is correct:
A Direct Connect gateway associated with gateways in all three Regions lets one pair of connections reach VPCs across Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hosted VIF per Region: unnecessary.
• Private VIF to VGWs in multiple Regions: a VIF attaches to one gateway.
• Transit VIF to VPCs directly: attaches to DX gateway.

Key takeaway: one DX, many Regions → DX gateway.
Q001701:
Why this is correct:
With BGP established, routes still won't reach the TGW route table unless propagation from the VPN attachment is enabled (or static routes added).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pending attachment: then tunnels wouldn't route at all.
• No VGW needed: TGW VPNs don't need one.
• Private ASN unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: BGP up ≠ routes propagated.
Q001702:
Why this is correct:
TGW ECMP across VPN connections requires BGP dynamic routing and equal-cost routes (same prefixes and AS path length), with ECMP support enabled on the TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accelerated VPN required: no.
• Same AZ: not applicable.
• Same CGW IP: not required.

Key takeaway: VPN ECMP = BGP + equal routes.
Q001703:
Why this is correct:
Aggressive DPD timers on the customer device during idle periods can tear down tunnels. Align DPD settings with AWS or keep traffic flowing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU fragmenting DPD: unlikely.
• PFS required for idle tunnels: no.
• AWS doesn't support DPD: it does.

Key takeaway: idle drops → DPD settings.
Q001704:
Why this is correct:
minimum_links sets how many member connections must be up for the LAG to stay operational.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MTU: unrelated.
• BFD only: detection, not LAG threshold.
• Remove connections: reduces capacity.

Key takeaway: LAG availability threshold → minimum_links.
Q001705:
Why this is correct:
AWS local preference BGP communities (high on the preferred VIF, low on the backup) control which VIF AWS uses to reach on-premises.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default route only: not the mechanism.
• Lower hold timer: detection only.
• Higher MED on preferred: makes it less preferred.

Key takeaway: steer AWS outbound → local preference communities.
Q001707:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer identified Subnet B's NACL as the blocker. Fix those NACL rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only SGs: it evaluates NACLs, routes, and more.
• Can't analyze load balancers: it can.
• DNS: it analyzes L3/L4 configuration.

Key takeaway: trust the component Reachability Analyzer names.
Q001708:
Why this is correct:
VPC Traffic Mirroring copies packets from ENIs to a target (such as an NLB or GWLB) fronting the IDS appliances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering: connectivity, not copies.
• Flow logs: metadata, not packets.
• PrivateLink: service access.

Key takeaway: packet copies for IDS → Traffic Mirroring.
Q001709:
Why this is correct:
Mirrored traffic arrives VXLAN-encapsulated on UDP 4789. The target's security group must allow it, and the tool must decapsulate it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VNI must match source: not the requirement.
• Same subnet required: no.
• Internet traffic only: no.

Key takeaway: mirror targets need UDP 4789 and VXLAN handling.
Q001710:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Network Monitor uses probes to measure latency and packet loss continuously along hybrid paths.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reachability Analyzer: static configuration.
• DX egress metric: throughput only.
• Internet Monitor: internet paths to users.

Key takeaway: hybrid path quality → Network Monitor.
Q001711:
Why this is correct:
pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr show the original packet addresses, revealing pre-NAT source and final destination alongside srcaddr and dstaddr.

Why the other options are wrong:
• dstaddr/srcaddr: interface-level addresses.
• flow-direction: direction only.

Key takeaway: see through NAT → pkt-* fields.
Q001714:
Why this is correct:
Each VPN tunnel supports about 1.25 Gbps. Exceeding it causes drops. Use ECMP across multiple tunnels or connections via TGW.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No per-tunnel limit: there is one.
• NACL: PacketDropCountNoRoute indicates routing.
• BGP flapping: would show state changes.

Key takeaway: VPN throughput → scale with ECMP.
Q001715:
Why this is correct:
Partitioning by account, Region, and date (with partition projection or Glue) lets Athena prune data and query efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift Spectrum required: no.
• Separate buckets: unnecessary.
• Unpartitioned table: scans everything.

Key takeaway: large log sets → partitions.
Q001716:
Why this is correct:
Mirror filter rules are evaluated from the lowest number. Rule 100 (reject TCP 22) matches first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accept before reject: no.
• OR combination: no.
• Can't filter ports: they can.

Key takeaway: lowest rule number first.
Q001717:
Why this is correct:
Network Monitor probes measure packet loss and latency on the path, revealing gray failures that connection state metrics miss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ConnectionState only: misses brownouts.
• Longer hold timer: hides issues.
• Wait for Health events: slow.

Key takeaway: brownouts → active probing.
Q001720:
Why this is correct:
Endpoint weights control the share of traffic within an endpoint group. Setting a lower weight on the new endpoint sends it less traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TCP health checks: not traffic control.
• Traffic dial 100% equal weights: no gradual shift.
• Source IP affinity: stickiness.

Key takeaway: within-group shares → endpoint weights.
Q001721:
Why this is correct:
IPsec overhead reduces the path MTU below 9001. Without working PMTUD or MSS clamping, oversized packets are dropped.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-tunnel throughput: different symptom.
• Raise on-prem to jumbo: VPN doesn't support it.
• Jumbo within one subnet only: false.

Key takeaway: VPN lowers path MTU.
Q001722:
Why this is correct:
Cross-AZ data transfer is charged. Routing requests to same-AZ replicas or cache nodes reduces cross-AZ traffic while keeping multi-AZ resilience.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs compress traffic: no.
• Single AZ: loses resilience.
• TGW free: no.

Key takeaway: AZ-aware routing reduces transfer costs.
Q001723:
Why this is correct:
A partner hosted connection at about 2 Gbps matches the needed capacity without paying for 10 Gbps or managing a LAG.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 10 Gbps always cheaper: overprovisioned.
• Hosted VIF provides cross-connect: incorrect.
• Two 1 Gbps in a LAG: more cost and complexity.

Key takeaway: right-size DX capacity.
Q001724:
Why this is correct:
Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP with static anycast IPs and health-based Regional failover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neither supports UDP: Global Accelerator does.
• Only cheaper: capability is the reason.
• CloudFront any protocol: HTTP(S) only.

Key takeaway: UDP multi-Region → Global Accelerator.
Q001725:
Why this is correct:
Large transfers hang when ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages are blocked, breaking PMTUD. Allow ICMP or clamp TCP MSS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS: unrelated.
• IKE lifetime: different symptom.
• Connection limits: not the cause.

Key takeaway: large transfers hang over VPN → PMTUD black hole.
Q001726:
Why this is correct:
A few DX connections shared via a Direct Connect gateway and Transit Gateway serve all accounts, reducing cost and complexity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Connection per account: expensive.
• Share EC2 via RAM: nonsensical.
• VPNs per account: not dedicated connectivity.

Key takeaway: share DX across accounts via DX gateway + TGW.
Q001727:
Why this is correct:
The traffic dial on an endpoint group controls the percentage of traffic directed to that Region's group.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Weights: share within a group.
• Health check interval: no.
• Source IP sampling: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: Regional traffic share → traffic dial.
Q001728:
Why this is correct:
Enhanced networking needs the ENA driver installed and current. Without it, instances don't reach their rated bandwidth.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DHCP options: DNS.
• NAT gateway: not the limit here.
• SG bandwidth limits: don't exist.

Key takeaway: high network throughput → ENA driver.
Q001729:
Why this is correct:
Data transfer out over Direct Connect has a lower per-GB rate than internet egress. At 500 TB per month, savings likely outweigh port-hour costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Free internet egress: false.
• Same rate: DX is lower.
• Free DX transfer: false.

Key takeaway: high egress volumes favor DX.
Q001731:
Why this is correct:
Strict rule order with explicit rule group priorities and a strict default action (such as drop established) makes evaluation predictable across groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One stateless group: loses stateful features.
• Alert only: doesn't enforce.
• Default action order: less predictable.

Key takeaway: predictable firewall policies → strict order.
Q001732:
Why this is correct:
Suricata-compatible IPS rules can match specific payload content and signatures, blocking malware traffic even when domains change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Domain lists: miss unknown or changing domains.
• 5-tuple rules detecting malware automatically: no.
• Stateless port rules: too coarse.

Key takeaway: content inspection → Suricata IPS rules.
Q001733:
Why this is correct:
Rule group capacity is fixed at creation. Create a larger group, migrate the rules, and update the policy to use it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duplicate names: not allowed.
• Support quota: capacity isn't a quota.
• Edit capacity: can't change.

Key takeaway: capacity is immutable → recreate larger.
Q001734:
Why this is correct:
If traffic arrives through a proxy or CDN, aggregating on IP counts the proxy's IP. Aggregate on a trusted forwarded-IP header to rate-limit real clients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Advanced: not rate limiting per client.
• Raise the limit: doesn't fix aggregation.
• Single global key: blocks everyone together.

Key takeaway: rate-limit the real client IP.
Q001735:
Why this is correct:
A Firewall Manager WAF policy applies the web ACL to every ALB across the organization, including new ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account ACLs with SCP: toil.
• RAM-shared web ACL: teams must associate manually.
• Config remediation: reactive.

Key takeaway: org-wide WAF → Firewall Manager.
Q001738:
Why this is correct:
Engaging the Shield Response Team requires Shield Advanced plus Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only with CloudFront: no.
• Trust & Safety case: no.
• Basic Support: not eligible.

Key takeaway: SRT needs a qualifying Support plan.
Q001739:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced protects only resources explicitly added as protected resources. The Elastic IP wasn't added.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EIPs ineligible: they're eligible.
• No UDP inspection: UDP attacks are covered.
• Automatic coverage: must add resources.

Key takeaway: add each resource to Shield Advanced.
Q001740:
Why this is correct:
NACLs are stateless, so responses to outbound requests need inbound rules for ephemeral ports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: NACLs have both.
• SGs stateless: they're stateful.
• Reverse order: lowest number first.

Key takeaway: stateless NACLs need return-port rules.
Q001742:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated lowest number first and the first match applies. Rule 50's range also covered legitimate traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound only: it's inbound.
• Inverts defaults: no.
• Most restrictive: first match wins.

Key takeaway: check NACL deny ranges and order.
Q001743:
Why this is correct:
A customer-managed prefix list holds all 200 CIDRs and is referenced in one security group rule, staying within quotas and easy to update.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unlimited rules: quotas exist.
• NACLs unlimited: also limited and stateless.
• 200 SGs: impractical.

Key takeaway: many CIDRs → prefix lists.
Q001744:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs don't capture traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver. Use Resolver query logging for DNS visibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Interval too long: not the reason.
• UDP excluded: flow logs include UDP.
• dns-query field: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: DNS visibility → Resolver query logs.
Q001745:
Why this is correct:
A custom flow log format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr shows the original instance addresses behind the NAT gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance ENI logs only: doesn't show post-NAT.
• 1-minute interval: unrelated.
• CloudWatch destination: unrelated.

Key takeaway: NAT visibility → pkt-* fields.
Q001746:
Why this is correct:
Athena can query Parquet flow logs with SQL, counting distinct destination ports per source among REJECTs in a time window to find scans.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena can't query Parquet: it can.
• Manual file search: impractical.
• WAF logging: HTTP only.

Key takeaway: detect port scans with Athena.
Q001748:
Why this is correct:
A single-Region trail misses events from other Regions. Make it multi-Region (and organization-wide).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Org trails can't capture EC2 networking: they can.
• Member must have own trail: org trails cover members.
• Requester's Region only: acceptance is logged where it happens.

Key takeaway: multi-Region trails capture all Regions.
Q001749:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress invokes a Lambda function that revokes port 3389 rules immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait for GuardDuty: exposure remains.
• 24-hour Config rule: slow.
• Flow logs: only after traffic.

Key takeaway: prevent exposure windows → event-driven remediation.
Q001751:
Why this is correct:
A custom Lambda-backed Config rule can call EC2 and Network Firewall APIs to check whether each VPC has an associated firewall.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Not possible with Config: custom rules make it possible.
• Conformance packs express any logic: no.
• Managed rule for this: none built specifically.

Key takeaway: custom checks → custom Config rules.
Q001752:
Why this is correct:
Remediation happens only if a remediation action (such as an SSM Automation document) is attached and automatic remediation is enabled.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom rules can't remediate: they can.
• Needs Security Hub: no.
• Config read-only: remediation actions exist.

Key takeaway: attach a remediation action.
Q001755:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty analyzes VPC flow logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail against threat intelligence, without agents, to detect C2 beaconing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs third-party feed: built-in.
• Network Firewall only: requires rule management.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: C2 detection → GuardDuty.
Q001756:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty consumes flow log, DNS, and CloudTrail data independently. You don't need to enable those logs yourself.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requires flow logs to S3: no.
• Only CloudTrail: no.
• Resolver logging required: no.

Key takeaway: GuardDuty reads its own data sources.
Q001757:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty sees DNS queries through the Amazon-provided resolver. Sending queries to a third-party resolver hides them from GuardDuty's DNS analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only flow logs affected: DNS analysis is affected.
• Inspects at the ENI: no.
• Redirects DNS: no.

Key takeaway: bypassing the VPC resolver reduces visibility.
Q001759:
Why this is correct:
Set the AWS tunnel options to allow only the approved encryption, integrity algorithms, DH groups, and IKE versions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CGW only: AWS side may accept weaker ones.
• Config rule blocking tunnels: not the mechanism.
• Defaults only AES-256: defaults include others.

Key takeaway: enforce crypto via tunnel options.
Q001760:
Why this is correct:
Frequent UP/DOWN cycling often comes from mismatched DPD timers. Align timeouts and retries on both sides.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Throughput limit: drops packets, not tunnels.
• Five-minute sessions: no.
• CGW IP change: tunnel wouldn't come back.

Key takeaway: flapping tunnels → check DPD.
Q001761:
Why this is correct:
VPN over DX is limited per tunnel (about 1.25 Gbps). MACsec encrypts at near line rate on supported dedicated connections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPN outperforms MACsec: no.
• Identical: no.
• MACsec unavailable on DX: it's available.

Key takeaway: line-rate DX encryption → MACsec.
Q001762:
Why this is correct:
MACsec isn't supported on hosted connections. It requires a supported dedicated connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Partner support case: no.
• Enable on AWS side first: still unsupported.
• Below 100 Gbps: 10 Gbps dedicated supports it.

Key takeaway: MACsec → dedicated connections.
Q001763:
Why this is correct:
MACsec uses a pre-shared CKN/CAK pair, and MKA derives and rotates the data encryption keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS manages all keys: you supply CKN/CAK.
• Re-enter at each rotation: MKA handles rotation.
• TLS certificates: not used.

Key takeaway: MACsec keys = CKN/CAK + MKA.
Q001764:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates for internal mTLS between services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM for private hostnames: not allowed.
• Cognito client certificates: no.
• Secrets Manager CA: doesn't exist.

Key takeaway: internal mTLS → Private CA.
Q001766:
Why this is correct:
DNS-validated ACM renewal needs the validation CNAME. Recreate it, or reissue the certificate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No ongoing validation: renewal validates again.
• Only HTTP-validated: no.
• Falls back to email: not automatically.

Key takeaway: keep validation CNAMEs.
Q001767:
Why this is correct:
Use public ACM certificates for the public website and AWS Private CA for internal hostnames.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Private CA for both: browsers won't trust it.
• Public ACM for internal names: validation isn't optional.
• IP-only certificates: no.

Key takeaway: public names → ACM; internal → Private CA.
Q001768:
Why this is correct:
PrivateLink to the provider's endpoint service keeps PHI traffic on the AWS network without internet exposure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS over internet: still internet.
• IGW with SGs: internet.
• Global Accelerator: public entry points.
• Public endpoint: internet.

Key takeaway: private third-party access → PrivateLink.
Q001769:
Why this is correct:
Private DNS for interface endpoints requires the VPC's enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames attributes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never override: private DNS does.
• SG outbound internet: no.
• Only Lambda: no.

Key takeaway: private DNS needs VPC DNS attributes.
Q001770:
Why this is correct:
PrivateLink exposes only the service endpoint, not full VPC reachability, and tolerates overlapping CIDRs. Peering connects whole networks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical security: no.
• Peering uses IPsec: no.
• Peering transitive and unlimited: no.

Key takeaway: least exposure → PrivateLink.
Q002073:
Why this is correct:
TGW peering doesn't support propagation. Add static routes to remote CIDRs pointing to the peering attachment in each TGW route table.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo frames: unrelated.
• BGP on peering: not supported.
• DX gateway: unrelated.

Key takeaway: TGW peering = static routes.
Q002074:
Why this is correct:
One transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway associated with the Transit Gateways gives all 80 VPCs access over one connection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VIF per VPC: VIF limits.
• Peering via one VPC: not transitive.
• Public VIF with VPN tunnels: complex.

Key takeaway: many VPCs over DX → transit VIF + DX gateway + TGW.
Q002075:
Why this is correct:
A PrivateLink endpoint service behind an NLB works with overlapping customer CIDRs and exposes only the TCP service.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public IPs: internet exposure.
• Shared TGW: overlapping CIDRs break routing.
• Peering: overlapping CIDRs not allowed.

Key takeaway: overlapping consumers → PrivateLink.
Q002076:
Why this is correct:
An origin group with primary and secondary origins fails over automatically on 5xx errors or timeouts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer timeouts: still fails.
• Two distributions with DNS: slower.
• Lambda@Edge rewrite: always uses secondary.

Key takeaway: CloudFront origin failover → origin groups.
Q002077:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall with AWS managed domain lists (malware, newly registered domains), deployed org-wide via Firewall Manager with logging, blocks resolution centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zones per domain: nonsense.
• NACLs by IP: IPs change.
• SG port 53: blocks all DNS.

Key takeaway: block malicious resolution org-wide → DNS Firewall + Firewall Manager.
Q002078:
Why this is correct:
The 7224:7300 community sets high local preference in AWS, making AWS prefer connection A for traffic to that prefix.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Community on B: wrong connection.
• Less specific on A: makes B preferred.
• Higher MED on A: makes A less preferred.

Key takeaway: prefer a DX path → 7224:7300 community.
Q002079:
Why this is correct:
MACsec on a dedicated 100 Gbps connection encrypts at line rate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single IPsec tunnel: throughput limited.
• Application TLS only: not all traffic.
• VPN over public VIF: throughput limited.

Key takeaway: line-rate encryption → MACsec.
Q002080:
Why this is correct:
Multiple BGP-routed VPN connections on a Transit Gateway with ECMP spread traffic beyond the per-tunnel limit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Acceleration alone: doesn't raise per-tunnel limit.
• VGW: no ECMP across connections.
• Static routing: no ECMP.

Key takeaway: VPN throughput → ECMP on TGW.
Q002081:
Why this is correct:
With overlapping CIDRs, PrivateLink (endpoint service in B, interface endpoint in A) exposes the API without routing between the VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TGW propagation: overlapping routes.
• Secondary CIDR alone: workloads still overlap.
• Peering: not allowed with overlaps.

Key takeaway: overlapping networks → PrivateLink.
Q002082:
Why this is correct:
An egress-only internet gateway allows outbound IPv6 connections and blocks inbound connections initiated from the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT gateway: IPv4 (NAT64 aside).
• VGW: VPN.
• IGW: allows inbound.

Key takeaway: IPv6 outbound only → egress-only IGW.
Q002083:
Why this is correct:
Reachability Analyzer traces the configured path across SGs, NACLs, route tables, and TGW, identifying the blocking component.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs: show results, not cause.
• Traffic Mirroring: packets.
• Network Monitor: latency and loss.

Key takeaway: find the blocking config → Reachability Analyzer.
Q002084:
Why this is correct:
Traffic Mirroring copies full packets to an NLB fronting the IDS, out of band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow Logs: metadata only.
• CloudTrail: API calls.
• GWLB inline: not out of band.

Key takeaway: out-of-band payload inspection → Traffic Mirroring.
Q002085:
Why this is correct:
A custom format with pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr shows the original instance IPs and final destinations through the NAT gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mirroring the NAT gateway: not supported.
• IGW flow logs: not available.
• NAT instance: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: see behind NAT → pkt-* fields.
Q002086:
Why this is correct:
Transit Gateway supports a maximum MTU of 8500 bytes. 9001-byte packets are dropped (or need PMTUD).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Jumbo only cross-Region peering: no.
• SGs drop fragments: no.
• 1500 only: TGW supports 8500.

Key takeaway: TGW MTU = 8500.
Q002087:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway in each AZ, with each AZ's route table pointing to its local NAT gateway, removes the single-AZ dependency and cross-AZ charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move instances to one AZ: loses resilience.
• More bandwidth: still single AZ.
• Egress-only IGW: IPv6 only.

Key takeaway: NAT gateway per AZ.
Q002088:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall TLS inspection decrypts outbound HTTPS using ACM certificates, inspects it, and re-encrypts.
